n: Despite his wealth and honor, Jehoshaphat formed a marriage alliance with wicked King Ahab of Israel — his son Jehoram married Ahab’s daughter Athaliah. This alliance would later nearly destroy David’s line.
Years later Jehoshaphat visited Ahab in Samaria. Ahab threw him a lavish feast and urged him to join an attack on Ramoth-gilead, a city east of the Jordan held by Syria.

f.g: A fortified town in Gilead, east of the Jordan, disputed between Israel and Syria.
Enticed or lured — the same Hebrew word used for ‘entice’ in v.19-21.

n: Jehoshaphat agreed: “I am as you are, my people as your people.” Too quickly he tied himself to an ungodly ally.
To his credit, Jehoshaphat insisted that they first ask the Lord what to do.

f.w: Inquire, I pray thee, at the word of the LORD

n: Ahab gathered 400 court prophets, who unanimously said, “Go — God will give it to you.” They told the king what he wanted to hear.
Jehoshaphat sensed something was wrong and asked whether there was a true prophet of the Lord they could consult.

f.w: a prophet of the LORD besides
f.g: Another prophet — one truly of the Lord.

n: Ahab admits there is one, Micaiah, but says he hates him because he never prophesies anything good for him. Jehoshaphat gently rebukes him.
Ahab sends an officer to bring Micaiah quickly.
The two kings sit in royal robes on thrones at the threshing floor by Samaria’s gate, while the prophets perform before them — an impressive public stage.

f.g: An open space — literally a threshing floor.

n: Zedekiah, one of the court prophets, makes iron horns as a dramatic sign: with these you will gore Syria to destruction.
All the prophets echo the same message: go up and succeed.
The messenger pressures Micaiah to agree with the others: everyone is saying good things — please do the same.
Micaiah’s answer is the mark of a true prophet: as the Lord lives, I will speak only what my God says.

f.w: what my God saith, that will I speak

n: When asked, Micaiah at first sarcastically repeats the false prophets’ words — go up and win. His tone must have made his mockery obvious.
Ahab sees through it and demands the truth in the Lord’s name. Ironically, he knows the truth when he hears it but refuses to obey it.
Micaiah’s true vision: Israel scattered on the mountains like sheep without a shepherd — meaning their king would die. Jesus later used this image for people without spiritual leadership.

f.w: as sheep that have no shepherd

n: Ahab turns to Jehoshaphat: “Didn’t I tell you he only predicts disaster for me?”
Micaiah describes a vision of God’s heavenly council: the Lord on His throne, surrounded by the hosts of heaven. True prophets testify of what they have seen in God’s council.

f.w: I saw the LORD sitting upon his throne

n: In the vision, the Lord asks who will lure Ahab into battle where he will fall. Various suggestions are made.
A spirit steps forward and offers to entice Ahab. The Lord asks how.

The spirit says it will be a lying spirit in the prophets’ mouths. The vision depicts God allowing Ahab’s chosen deception to lead him to the judgment he had earned — Ahab wanted lies and received them.

f.w: a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets
f.g: A vivid prophetic picture; scripture elsewhere teaches God does not lie but permits those who reject truth to believe falsehood.

n: Micaiah applies the vision: your prophets are deceived, and the Lord has decreed disaster for you.
Zedekiah slaps Micaiah and sneers: “Which way did the Spirit of the Lord go from me to talk to you?”
Micaiah replies that Zedekiah will find out when he hides in an inner room on the day disaster strikes.

f.g: A back room — a place to hide in fear.

n: Ahab orders Micaiah taken to the city governor Amon and to Joash the king’s son.
He commands that Micaiah be imprisoned on minimal bread and water until Ahab returns safely.

f.g: Prison rations — barely enough to survive.

n: Micaiah stakes his credibility: if you return safely, the Lord has not spoken through me. He calls all the people to witness. This is the biblical test of a prophet.

f.w: then hath not the LORD spoken by me

n: Despite the warning, both kings go up to Ramoth-gilead.
Ahab tries to outwit the prophecy by disguising himself as an ordinary soldier, while Jehoshaphat wears his royal robes — making Jehoshaphat the obvious target.
The Syrian king had ordered his chariot commanders to target only Israel’s king.

f.g: Anyone, of low or high rank.

n: Seeing Jehoshaphat’s robes, the Syrians surround him, thinking he is Ahab. Jehoshaphat cries out, and the Lord helps him by turning them away. Chronicles adds that God moved them.
Realizing he wasn’t Israel’s king, the commanders stopped pursuing him.
A soldier shot an arrow at random, and it struck Ahab through a gap in his armor. No disguise can hide anyone from God’s word.

f.g: At random, without a particular aim.
A gap between plates of the armor.

n: As the battle raged, Ahab was propped up in his chariot facing the Syrians until evening, and he died at sunset — fulfilling Micaiah’s prophecy exactly.
